title: The Best Summer
summary: Tamra Davis discusses The Best Summer, the documentary she assembled from rediscovered footage of the Summersault festival. She reflects on filming musicians away from the stage and revisiting the backstage friendships captured on her camcorder.
transcript:
Tamra Davis spoke with Lauren Taylor remotely, ahead of her visit to Melbourne as a guest of MIFF, where The Best Summer screens in the Music on Film program. Broadcast on Breaking and Entering, Triple R, 30 July 2026.

Lauren: She did make a name for herself originally by directing music videos for Sonic Youth and The Smiths and Young MC, even Bette Midler. Her feature film directorial credits include Adam Sandler's breakout film, Billy Madison, Britney Spears' road trip feature, Crossroads, and also her acclaimed documentary, Jean-Michel Basquiat: The Radiant Child. Tamra's going to be heading to Australia very soon, next week in fact, from Los Angeles as a special guest of MIFF. Her new archival documentary, The Best Summer, is screening as part of the Music on Film program that is, of course, presented by RRR.

It's a really remarkable, accidental time capsule of 90s alternative music culture. When Tamra was evacuating her Malibu home during the 2025 wildfires, she uncovered a box of unmarked videotapes. And what she found inside was raw, unedited footage from the 1995 Summersault Festival here in Australia. I imagine many RRR listeners would remember that iconic festival. The lineup included acts like Beastie Boys, Sonic Youth, Beck, Bikini Kill, Pavement, Kim Deal's Breeders-hiatus project, The Amps, and what was at the time Dave Grohl's very new band, Foo Fighters, as well. At the time, Tamra was newly married to her husband, Mike D of the Beastie Boys, and brought her camcorder along on tour, capturing an extraordinary and intimate look at these now era-defining artists at the peak of their youth, in a much simpler time before smartphones and social media.

At the heart of the documentary is riot grrrl icon Kathleen Hanna from Bikini Kill, who is equipped with a microphone and conducts these playfully candid, unfiltered interviews with her fellow artists backstage. The film also completely bypasses traditional talking-head narration, and as a result, the footage really speaks for itself. Tamra captures these really rare moments of community and creative transition with really raw energy. And I began the interview with Tamra Davis by asking her to take us back to that moment when she first discovered the footage and realised she had a whole documentary that was just sitting in a box.

Tamra: Yeah, I found this box of tapes. I have so many tapes; I've been filming kind of my whole life. And so I was like, I should get something done with them, because I was moving from a fire, and I was like, oh my God, I should get them digitised or something. And so then I was like, what's on these tapes? They just had scribbles on them or something. And so I had to buy a camera. So first I bought a camera to put them in, before I just went and digitised everything, because it's expensive. And then I just saw this beautiful little one-inch square frame. And I was like, what? There's pictures. I didn't know I shot the Foo Fighters, or I didn't know I did interviews. And I kept taking pictures, and even videos, of the little screen off the old video camera, because I just couldn't believe I had this really beautiful old footage, and the quality of it. It had such beautiful lighting, and I had no idea that I shot this whole festival. And I had so much footage, with all the interviews and everything. It's pretty incredible.

Lauren: Can you take us back to 1995? You're riding high on the success of your film, Billy Madison. You're married to Mike D from the Beastie Boys. You've asked to jump on this tour, Summersault, which is a new festival created as a rival festival to Big Day Out by Steve Pavlovic, who famously went on to found Modular Records. Can you tell me about your decision to head to Australia at that time? Did you know specifically you wanted to document this tour?

Tamra: No, I think it was more like, Mike and I had already been together for maybe 10 years, and I was a pretty well-known music video director. Billy Madison was my third movie. And so I was kind of known as a filmmaker, and I'd made videos for some of these bands. A lot of them were my friends as well. Mike and I got married, I think it was 93, so we got married just right before this.

If you've married somebody who's a musician, they tour a lot. And so if you want to see them, you kind of have to go on the road with them. And because I was in between making a movie, I was like, oh, this is a perfect time for me to join and go on the road with Mike. And I love going on the road. It's so fun. It was so fun at that time, just seeing them play. And I just always had cameras with me wherever I went. So I was like, oh, if I'm going to see them, I'm always going to film Beastie Boys stuff. But yes, it was just more like that: if I'm going to go on the road and be with Mike, I have so much fun hanging out, but it just gives me something to do, to also be filming. It's a nice, fun hobby. It's like I brought my paints with me, or I brought a notebook to write. It's just kind of the thing that I always do.

Lauren: The artists in this documentary have this really wonderful unguardedness to them. We're getting to see these alternative rock icons in a really unusually relaxed state. Kathleen Hanna's mentioned recently that back then you didn't have to carry the weight of self-consciousness, because you weren't constantly on camera. How do you think the presence of smartphones and social media today changes how artists express themselves? And do you think you'd be able to capture the same energy in today's modern digital age?

Tamra: I feel like a lot of it is not so much the camera, but it's also the relationship with the people. I knew all those people. And when you're friends with people, and also if you're a director, I feel like it's all about getting a certain kind of performance from somebody. And so I wanted that super casual thing. I wasn't trying to do interviews like, hi, can you meet me in your dressing room, where I have a tripod and a couple of lights, and I'm going to sit there next to the camera and ask you questions. It was a very different situation. So I think if I knew the people, I feel like I could get a similar thing, if they were all my friends. It wasn't just that they were my friends; everybody was friends. And I feel like that was also part of it. Pav really kind of put the lineup together based on all his friends, and so we were all people that were hanging out with each other all the time anyway.

Lauren: In the documentary, you and Kathleen Hanna tag-team these interviews using what you call these Tiger Beat teenybopper questions, like: what's your favourite colour? What's your favourite food? Strangely, you did get some revealing answers from these artists, from those questions. Can you tell me about the decision to ask what might be considered easier or trivial or light-hearted questions to these musicians at the time?

Tamra: Kathleen remembers more than I do. I think she saw some people doing an interview, some guys, and she was like, we could do so much better than that. And I was like, yeah, let's do it. And I'm pretty sure what happened is I'm the weirdo that just took my ticket stub. It was written on my airline ticket stub, my questions. And I was like, okay, let's write out some questions, just really kind of girly, goofy, just playing. And then I had my questions, and then she decided to be like, I have some serious questions. The Kathleen questions I thought were so interesting, because she really wanted to know the difference between real life and a persona. And so her questions were actually quite profound, and mine were the loosen-up questions. And even so, you get a personality from the artists from that. But I feel like her questions, she really wanted to know those things.

Lauren: Looking back, it was a genius move to get Kathleen Hanna doing those interviews as well.

Tamra: She's the best.

Lauren: There's some fascinating conversations going on, as you mentioned, about stage personas and criticism. What is it about Kathleen Hanna in particular that you think makes the artists really open up in these interviews?

Tamra: She's such a star. She's so exceptional. I mean, I love her. I made a whole movie about her. I just think she's so fascinating. And on that tour, a lot of people hadn't really seen them play live and seen what Bikini Kill was about. And I really tried to show everybody standing on the side of the stage, because they were kind of the baby band. They were one of the first bands up. And so I was just enamoured with her. I thought she was hilarious. Kim Gordon and I were both obsessed with her, and we were trying to matchmake her and Adam, because we wanted her more in our lives. So we were like, let's see if her and Adam, they seem so funny together. Nobody would realise how great they would be together.

Lauren: It was amazing to see that play out. As you mentioned, this film accidentally captures the spark of the early romance between Kathleen Hanna and Ad-Rock, who became a couple soon after Summersault ended. I found this film a really interesting companion piece to two recent memoirs as well: Kathleen Hanna's Rebel Girl, but also Ione Skye's memoir, Say Anything. It was interesting getting to read about it from both their perspectives, but also now to see this captured on film as well. Did you feel a similar way?

Tamra: Totally. I mean, it's funny, because I really loved Ione's book. I thought it was really wonderful and vulnerable. And I was like, oh man, this is the tour that he comes back from, when she's at the house. Because I was there; I know all that stuff. So I was like, man, that's crazy. And then the same thing with Kathleen: she doesn't really talk that much about Adam in her book, but that was when they fell in love.

When I first did a cut, I had this format in mind when I put it together, this day-to-day thing, like day one or day two. And I did a first version, and I had a voiceover that kind of put context to stuff. I was like, oh, this is amazing to see Adam, so sad he's not with us. I was adding little things. And the first person I showed it to was Kim Gordon. And Kim Gordon just was like, stop talking. You're distracting me. She's like, why are you adding all this voice from the future coming into the past? And I was like, oh my God. And so she was like, just take it out. Nobody needs to know any of everybody. They'll either know or they won't, or they'll Google it. And it was a really smart thing, because I feel like we're so overburdened with, let me give you a billion more pieces of information. If people are interested, they'll look it up. And otherwise, they already know when you're watching a movie. When you know a fact and you start to see it and uncover, it was more powerful than me trying to tell you these things.

And I showed it to my kids and their generation. They're all in their 20s, and all their friends are in their 20s. And I got a lot of feedback from them, and they didn't want all the commentary. They wanted to discover it themselves. They didn't want it to be like, somebody says a great line and then it cuts to some information that you should know. They liked that it was kind of mysterious like that, and they'd have to find out if they were interested.

Lauren: One of the fascinating aspects, and there are many, is seeing this really raw 1995 evolution of Dave Grohl, watching it now. It's really striking to realise that this was filmed just a year after Kurt Cobain had passed away, capturing Dave in this really intensely vulnerable moment where he's still finding his feet with Foo Fighters. He openly admits how much he hates singing and hates talking to the audience, which feels like this weird alternative reality compared to the stadium-commanding Dave Grohl that we know today. Looking back, how do you view that footage now, in contrast to his massive career evolution?

Tamra: I know. It's funny, because he's like, yeah, what if it doesn't work out a few years later? And you're like, oh my God, you're still at it. I think it's amazing to see. I've known Dave from early days Nirvana all the way to now. They're all still managed by the same manager, and so we see each other here and there. And I think it's just so beautiful to see him find his voice in the film: by the end of it, he's telling the crowd how much he loves them. But getting through that time, and having the support of this community, I feel like that's really present in there.

I see that, but I also see — I showed it to his kids, and seeing their reaction to it is also beautiful to me, and how they never saw their dad like that. That to me is also interesting, and also one of the reasons why I made the film is I was like, man, my kids have never really seen their dad the way I saw their dad. They saw the Spike movie, but that's very different, in a very different context. I was like, yeah, look at this. This is your dad. I wanted them to see that as well.

[Unclear audio at 00:13:21–00:17:20]

Lauren: A lot of music festival culture from the early 90s really had that hyper-masculine energy to it as well, and with the lineups too. But your lens gives us this really beautiful, almost feminist subtext to the film. You're behind the camera. Kathleen's doing the interviews. There's Kim Gordon navigating the realities of motherhood and life on the road. When you first dug up those tapes, did you immediately recognise how radical it was to have that documented in that era?

Tamra: It was actually something I was looking for, because it had happened recently that I showed a short film I made. I made a feature on Jean-Michel Basquiat, but I have a short that's just the footage of him and I talking, and me being in the studio with him. And afterwards, all these women came up to me talking about how they saw how he talked to me, and how the female gaze really affected his performance and how he spoke, and his honesty and vulnerability, and how powerful that was. So to me, I was like, wow, this is really interesting. When I looked at my film, I was like, you can really see the female gaze, and the way everybody talks to me and Kathleen... It's different and it's powerful. And that's the thing as a young girl filming when I started out, and even to now: it's so hard to be a female filmmaker. The stats are even worse than they were before. And so I'm trying to show that, yeah, we're different, but look at the strengths of this. And that was the thing I really wanted to show: yeah, it's difficult to be a female filmmaker, but when you give us a camera and you give us an opportunity, look at the strengths that we also have.

That's also part of it. It's not just, oh, there's no difference. It's like, yeah, sometimes there is a difference, and it's actually really fucking amazing. It's good. And that [Unclear audio] shot an entire movie. I just look at that and I'm like, yeah, this whole movie shot just by one girl. And I want girls to be inspired by that. And I think that there is something about the female gaze, and what my eye goes to on the stage. And the flirty, kind of, that I have with people that are just whatever. It's more like fun. It's not like dude upon dude. I like leaning into that. I think there's something really strong about that. And I hope it inspires people, not just girls, but also people that are different. Knowing that you're who you are as an individual is authentic, and it affects the tone of your film.

Lauren: Kathleen Hanna's described you as someone that just makes things happen. Is that fearless quality something that resonates with you about yourself?

Tamra: I think so. I mean, I feel like you can't do the things I've done without making things happen. You have to just be like, okay, I'm going to make a film, or okay, I'm going to shoot this, or okay. You have to be super ambitious like that. I am pretty fearless in that way. But I think that's what I liked about Kathleen and I: even though we're very different people and come from different places, we both have that energy that's like, yeah, let's start a band. Let's make a movie. Let's shoot a documentary. I'm like, okay. She didn't become who she was because she didn't have that energy as well. And I think when you find another friend like that at a summer camp, that energy is just really special. And when you find that in another person, guy, girl, whoever, that's what gets things done. That's how you start bands, how you make movies, how you create a scene.

Lauren: You've captured some really incredible onstage performances as well. There are scenes of Sonic Youth on stage with those strobe lights almost covering the band members in these flashes of lightning. And there's Dave Grohl running out to stage with the Beastie Boys, screaming on 'Sabotage'. When you sent the film to these bands to approve, what was their reaction? Did they appreciate those moments being so lovingly preserved in that way?

Tamra: Yeah. I feel like they loved it just as much as me, because first of all, there's nothing like seeing yourself from 30 years ago, and you're gorgeous. Everybody looks good 30 years ago. We're all babies, but so cute. And the fashion is so good. And I am such a fan. I'm one of their biggest fans. So I shoot it with the love of a fan. My eye is if I was in the front row shooting it, and I'm shooting my favourite people and what I want to look at. So when you see Sonic Youth, I pretty much have the camera on Kim Gordon most of the time. I just think she's so amazing to look at, always. And yes, [Unclear audio] Thurston's incredible as well, but I'm always like, oh my God, Kim, how does she do it with those shoes? Panning down to her feet. So I feel like everyone really loved it.

And in the end, I think Kim was really right. I think everybody liked that. I didn't add anything in, because there wasn't anything controversial about it. It was like, this is who everybody was, what everybody said and what the music was like. Everybody approved it. That process went very well. And if anybody had a note, Mike, that was my favourite thing: I felt like I was happy to do a note, whatever it could possibly be, even just because it felt more like a collaboration. I've been working on projects where you get notes always from your executives, and those are different kinds of notes. So I liked showing it to them, knowing that if anybody had anything, or any comments, it was so easy to do. And I loved it.

Lauren: You mentioned Dave Grohl's kids seeing the film. I understand for the early screenings of the film, Kim Gordon and Steve Malkmus were in the audience, sitting next to their daughters as well, who are featured as babies in the documentary. Can you tell me more about how it felt to watch the film on the big screen? And these must've been special moments for those artists too, to share with their kids.

Tamra: Yeah. Watching it sitting next to Coco, who's in the film as a baby, and Kim was just so beautiful. It was one of the most incredible experiences. And I think also for Coco to see her life framed like that, how loving her parents were, and how her mom — it just was a beautiful way to see your life. I think it really helped her. It was such a wonderful way to see your childhood. Everyone loved you. You were so taken care of. And I think also Lottie, Steven's daughter: she came and spent a summer with us. She was one of the first persons I showed it to as well. So for her to see her dad at that time, it was really important to me.

[names uncertain] She was one of the first people to see it. I know all these kids now, and they're the next generation. They're all making music and doing cool, creative things. And I mean, for my boys, this was one of their favourite films that I've done. I'm like, really? This is your favourite? And they're like, yeah, by far, this is our favourite film. I was like, thanks. I guess that's a compliment.

Lauren: You screened it in Sydney. You're about to screen it in Melbourne. How does it feel getting to show this film on the big screen? Especially to Australian audiences who were perhaps there for Summersault in 1995.

Tamra: Yeah. There was a moment that I asked the audience who was there, and like half the audience raised their hand. It made me so excited, because they were there as well. And I feel like it's a shared experience. It's one of the strange things that happens on the film: it's all point of view. So you hear my voice, but I'm not really a presence. I really tried to make it feel like it's your experience. I didn't want it to be about me. I wanted it to be about a person's point of view. So I'm hoping that the people had that similar experience, or to me, it's almost like the fantasy version of the perfect experience, 'cause now you've got to go backstage with all those people that you saw.

We don't have a film like this for that time. There's Woodstock 99, but that's like a horror film as far as I'm concerned. I was trying to make the opposite of that. So I was just like, yeah, these bands are so important for our culture, and the evolution of music. And I'm just so happy that I had this footage. I'm so grateful. Also, sometimes it takes 30 years. If I made it then, I don't know if it would have been the film it is now. So I think there's something really cool about art: sometimes a painting, a piece of art, sometimes things take a little while before it finds itself.

Lauren: Thank you very much for this film and for the chat today. And we're looking forward to seeing you in Melbourne soon. Of course, you're a guest of MIFF for the festival.

Tamra: Thank you, and so nice talking with you. I can't wait to see you in Melbourne. I can't wait to be there.
